News Release
Wood Mackenzie projects EU inverter restrictions could cut forecast solar and storage installations at least 5% in Central and Eastern Europe through 2030

26 November 2026
6 minute read

Email
Share by email

In April 2026, the European Commission restricted "high-risk" inverters from all solar and storage projects receiving loans from EU institutions or direct EU funding. With the 1 November 2026 grandfathering deadline now in the past, Wood Mackenzie estimates that over 21 GW of European solar PV inverter demand will be exposed to these restrictions between 2027 and 2030. Utility-scale solar and storage projects receiving EU financing make up a majority of exposed capacity.
The European Commission's decision came as a response to growing cybersecurity and supply-chain concerns brewing across the region. These restrictions are expected to be followed by broader provisions to protect critical grid infrastructure through upcoming policies, including the Cyber Security Act. However, the timing and scope of implementation of these initial funding restrictions have introduced uncertainty and supply chain challenges into the market.
Notably, all inverter manufacturers headquartered in China will be impacted through the country’s “high-risk” designation. Chinese suppliers accounted for over 80% of inverter shipments to Europe in 2025, with even higher market shares in price-sensitive markets that rely most heavily on EU financial support. Given this deep structural dependency, cybersecurity or trade measures that restrict “high-risk” inverter procurement will drastically reshape Europe’s inverter supply landscape.
To understand these changes, Wood Mackenzie spoke with or received survey results from more than 30 industry stakeholders, including suppliers, distributors, solar and storage developers, European national solar associations in countries with high exposure to EU-supported loans or funding. The study aimed to understand how stakeholders perceive product availability, price increases, and contract renegotiations after the ban, and how that could impact solar and storage deployments in the coming years.
“Western inverter vendors will need to play a significant role in mitigating supply chain shortages and enabling a majority of exposed projects to continue on schedule,” said Joe Shangraw, Inverter Supply Chain Analyst at Wood Mackenzie. “We estimate that non-high-risk inverter manufacturing capacity available to the European market will exceed 150 GW by the end of 2027. This should be adequate to fulfil the region’s solar and storage inverter demand. However, our research revealed several key ways in which western vendors haven’t yet aligned with the needs of stakeholders, especially in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE)”.
“The Central and Eastern Europe region faces significantly higher exposure to current EU inverter restrictions, as well as a potential full ban as a result of upcoming Cyber Security Act revisions,” said Juan Monge, Principal Analyst, Wood Mackenzie. “This is because a higher share of projects here relies on EU loans and funding than elsewhere in the EU, and because Chinese inverter vendors have dominated these highly price-sensitive markets and have established strong sales and after sales infrastructure”.
Stakeholders in CEE reported a disconnect between these manufacturing figures and localized product availability. Some reported that it could take months or even years for western inverter vendors to develop adequate infrastructure to support sales and after-sales services, even for those already certified to sell to their country. Longer lead times for large purchase orders could also delay large-scale projects.
Even as western vendors make necessary business expansions, Wood Mackenzie expects price sensitivity to be a leading contributor to demand attrition. Some project developers reported that cost increases as low as 1-5% could be detrimental to already razor-thin margins. Even though inverters are a small portion of total costs, system-level price premiums for PV and storage projects can increase by between 2-10% as a result of inverter changes.
Key findings

Over 21 GW of European PV inverter demand and 13 GW of storage inverter demand face exposure to the restrictions between 2027 and 2030. Approximately 14% of European PV projects and 10% of storage projects are reliant on EU-backed loans and funding.
Across major CEE markets, Wood Mackenzie estimates in its base case forecast that 2027-2030 PV installations could decline by an average of 6%, and storage deployments could see a reduction of 5% compared to pre-restriction market conditions. Romania, Czechia, and Bulgaria are most impacted due to high exposure to funding restrictions.
Across all of Europe, the four-year forecast for solar and storage will only decline by 3%, as major markets in Western Europe have more price flexibility and stronger relationships with non-high-risk inverter vendors. Forecast reductions are concentrated in 2027 when western inverter supply chains are still least mature.
Wood Mackenzie also considered a high-severity impact scenario modelling a full EU-wide ban on “high-risk” inverters. Due to pricing challenges and sweeping supply chain overhauls, forecast four-year CEE installation losses exceed 18% for solar and 13% for energy storage. At an EU-wide level, solar declines are lower in this high-severity impact scenario, 11% for solar and 13% for storage, with the heaviest losses concentrated after implementation in 2029-2030.
Market challenges extend beyond direct inverter procurement. The most popular energy storage products in Europe are sold as AC-blocks, integrating the battery and inverter from a single vendor. The need to decouple Chinese integrated solutions will increase average prices and complicate installation and warranty processes.  Additionally, EPCs and installers in CEE claimed that they will face a cost burden to train staff to work with unfamiliar models.

Background and Methodology
At the time of publishing, the European Commission has not officially released a press statement or official document outlining the details of the April 2026 decision; Wood Mackenzie’s understanding of the restrictions comes from public statements, press releases, and our conversations with industry stakeholders.
This publicly available report was commissioned by SolarPower Europe. Wood Mackenzie presents its own independent findings as a result of our internal modelling and surveying of both the scope and impacts of inverter restrictions.
Two separate models were prepared for this study. The base case reflects current European Commission restrictions on EU-funded projects and no further restrictions on the private sector. The high-severity scenario applies a strict interpretation of possible language of the upcoming Cyber Security Act by extending a ban of “high-risk” inverters to all new projects regardless of funding source, officially enforced by 2029. Wood Mackenzie does not make policy recommendations based on the findings of this analysis.
